clinicalPearls: Presents with recurrent episodes of flaccid limb weakness that spare the respiratory and bulbar muscles in most attacks, with preserved consciousness throughout
Attacks are typically triggered by rest following vigorous exercise and by carbohydrate-rich meals, and often begin in the second or third decade
Serum potassium falls during an attack because of an intracellular potassium shift, not a true whole-body deficit, so aggressive supplementation risks rebound hyperkalaemia

Most cases are autosomal dominant with reduced penetrance, more clinically apparent in males, and are caused by mutations in the CACNA1S calcium channel gene or, less often, the SCN4A sodium channel gene
A thyrotoxic form clinically mimics the hereditary disease and should be excluded, particularly in patients of Asian ancestry
Long-term management centres on trigger avoidance, potassium-sparing strategies and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors used as prophylaxis
A fixed proximal vacuolar myopathy can develop over decades independent of attack frequency, sometimes as the dominant late feature
reference.pathophysiology: Hypokalaemic periodic paralysis arises from mutations in genes encoding skeletal-muscle voltage-gated ion channels, most commonly the dihydropyridine receptor calcium channel (CACNA1S) and less often the sodium channel (SCN4A). Many disease-causing variants affect arginine residues in the voltage-sensing domains, creating an aberrant gating-pore current that leaks cations through the sensor. During provocation, an insulin- or catecholamine-driven shift of potassium into muscle cells combines with this abnormal leak to paradoxically depolarise and then inactivate the sarcolemma, rendering the fibre inexcitable and producing flaccid weakness. The transient low serum potassium reflects redistribution rather than depletion, and repeated depolarisation over years may contribute to the vacuolar myopathy seen in some patients.
additionalDifferentials: Secondary hypokalaemia from renal or gastrointestinal potassium loss (e.g. renal tubular disorders, diuretics, vomiting)
Guillain-Barre syndrome and other acute flaccid weakness
Myasthenia gravis and other neuromuscular transmission disorders
additionalInvestigations: Serum potassium measured during a spontaneous attack, ideally with paired baseline values
Thyroid function tests to exclude thyrotoxic periodic paralysis
Electrocardiogram to detect hypokalaemic changes and to screen for the QU features of Andersen-Tawil syndrome
Prolonged (long) exercise electromyography protocol showing a post-exercise decrement in compound muscle action potential amplitude
Targeted genetic testing of CACNA1S and SCN4A
Muscle biopsy where a fixed myopathy is suspected, looking for tubular aggregates or vacuolar change
redFlags: Respiratory or bulbar involvement or unusually severe generalised paralysis during an attack
Cardiac arrhythmia or marked electrocardiographic disturbance during potassium shifts
Rebound hyperkalaemia following overzealous potassium replacement
Progressive fixed proximal weakness suggesting an established vacuolar myopathy
reference.prognosis: Attack frequency often lessens with age and with effective prophylaxis, and most patients have a normal lifespan, but a proportion develop a slowly progressive fixed proximal myopathy that can cause lasting disability independent of the acute episodes.
pitfalls: Assuming a true potassium deficit and over-replacing, which can precipitate dangerous rebound hyperkalaemia
Overlooking thyrotoxic periodic paralysis, a treatable acquired mimic
Relying on interictal potassium and creatine kinase, which are frequently normal between attacks
Missing the association with certain general anaesthetic and glucose-loading situations that can provoke attacks
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Abort acute attacks with oral potassium, giving carefully titrated intravenous potassium only for severe weakness, since the low potassium reflects redistribution and over-replacement risks rebound hyperkalaemia
Counsel strict avoidance of triggers, chiefly carbohydrate-rich meals and rest after vigorous exercise
Use carbonic anhydrase inhibitors such as acetazolamide or dichlorphenamide as the mainstay of prophylaxis
Consider potassium-sparing diuretics and a low-carbohydrate, low-sodium diet as adjunctive prevention
Exclude thyrotoxic periodic paralysis and treat any underlying thyrotoxicosis, especially in patients of Asian ancestry
Monitor for a slowly progressive fixed proximal myopathy and support with physiotherapy
Provide anaesthetic precautions and offer genetic counselling for this autosomal dominant CACNA1S or SCN4A channelopathy
